system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2172-02-18 19:56:00 to 2172-02-21 09:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted after experiencing persistent abdominal pain and increased discharge from her G-tube following an incident where she stepped on the tube. Initial evaluation raised concern for possible dislodgement or perforation, so she was kept NPO and underwent a G-tube sinogram, which confirmed the tube was correctly positioned with no evidence of leakage. She was restarted on tube feeds, which she tolerated well, and her skin erythema improved with proper wound care. Pain was managed with medication, and she remained stable throughout the admission. She was discharged home with instructions for ongoing wound care, medication management, and follow-up with surgery clinic for possible tube repositioning.
problems: Other specified procedures as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  History of bypass surgery with G tube in place, now with
hypoglycemia.  Assess tube placement.

TECHNIQUE:  2 supine AP views of the abdomen were obtained, before after the
administration of oral contrast material through the existing gastric tube.  

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:

Initial scout AP view of the abdomen demonstrates a catheter with tip
projecting over the left upper quadrant of the abdomen.  There is mild gaseous
distention of the colon which is also filled with a large amount of stool. 
After the injection of oral contrast material through the existing tube, there
is opacification of the body of the stomach and proximal loops of small bowel,
similar to that seen on the prior exam.  There is no evidence of extraluminal
contrast.

IMPRESSION:

G-tube located within the stomach with no evidence of extraluminal contrast.

HISTORY:  ___ female with refractory hypoglycemia requiring continuous
tube feeds.  Evaluate for passage of contrast.

COMPARISON:  G-tube check dated ___ and plain film of the abdomen
dated ___.

FINDINGS:

Two supine frontal views of the abdomen demonstrate contrast seen throughout
the colon and the rectum.  There is gas in nondistended loops of large and
small bowel without evidence of ileus or obstruction.  The colon contains a
large amount of stool.  The G-tube is seen projecting over the left upper
quadrant.  Suture material from prior gastric surgery is re-identified. 
Visualized osseous structures are unremarkable.  There are multiple
phleboliths in the pelvis.

IMPRESSION:

Interval passage of contrast into the colon and rectum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the bariatric team doctors. You came in tonight because of low blood sugar—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up this morning feeling really shaky and confused. My glucose monitor alarm went off—it said my blood sugar was 43.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s quite low. Did you treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took my sugar pills right away. I felt better after a few minutes, but then it happened again later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. We’re going to keep an eye on your levels. You also mentioned increased drainage around your G-tube and some pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the site has been leaking more than usual. I’m changing the dressing twice a day now because it gets soaked. And it’s tender—more than normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that. We’ve ordered a scan to make sure your tube is still in the right place and not leaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it possible the feeds are backing up into the bag? I’ve been worried the pump isn’t delivering them properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. The scan will help us see how the contrast moves. If it’s refluxing, we’ll adjust your setup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your abdominal X-ray with contrast shows the G-tube is correctly placed in the stomach. No leakage outside the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube is okay? But why am I having these lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube is working, but we think your hypoglycemia might be related to bacterial overgrowth in your intestines. You’ve had that before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from my breath test. So that could be causing the lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Bacteria can ferment carbs and trigger insulin release. We’re restarting your Flagyl to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the soreness at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some granulation tissue—extra tissue that sometimes grows around tubes. It can cause irritation and drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s common. We’ll treat it with silver nitrate to reduce it and prescribe an ointment called Bactroban to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugars have been stable overnight—between 80 and 110. No episodes of hypoglycemia so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean the Flagyl is working already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s early, but staying on your feeds and being in a controlled setting helps. Your endocrinologist wants a fasting test to check what’s driving the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fasting test? But I need my tube feeds to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it carefully. We’ll stop the feeds and monitor your blood sugar every hour. When it drops to around 55, we’ll draw blood to check insulin, C-peptide, and other levels, then restart your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And that will tell us why I’m having lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It helps distinguish if it’s from too much insulin production, reactive hypoglycemia, or something else. Your endocrinologist will review the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the fasting test this morning. You went about 12 hours without feeds. Your blood sugar dropped to 55, and we got the labs right then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did I do? Did I pass out or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you stayed alert the whole time. Nurses checked you every hour. All the labs were sent to your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And the contrast study this morning—what did that show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The contrast moved all the way into your colon and rectum. That means your digestive tract is open and functioning—no blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So everything’s moving like it should?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your tube site is looking better after treatment. We’ll keep using the silver nitrate and Bactroban ointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Another good night—your sugars stayed between 55 and 110. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your tube feeds as before. Take Flagyl three times a day for the bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds—octreotide and acarbose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Octreotide helps reduce insulin spikes, and acarbose slows sugar absorption. They may help prevent lows after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Apply the Bactroban ointment twice a day to the granulation tissue. Keep the dressing clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I have my follow-up with Dr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll review your test results and adjust your plan if needed. We’ll send them all the labs from the fasting test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—vitals stable, sugars in range. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any last instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds as prescribed. Use glucose tablets if your sugar drops. And call if you have fever, redness, or increased pain at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel shaky again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your sugar. If it’s low, treat it with glucose and sit down. If it doesn’t improve, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I feel much better knowing we’re on top of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send prescriptions for Flagyl, Bactroban, and the new meds. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one more thing—should I keep checking my blood sugar at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially before meals and at bedtime. And any time you feel shaky or confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted due to recurrent hypoglycemia with a blood glucose of 43, accompanied by increased drainage and pain at her G-tube site. Imaging confirmed the G-tube was correctly positioned with no leakage, and contrast passed normally into the colon. She was restarted on metronidazole for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, which may contribute to hypoglycemia. Granulation tissue at the G-tube site was treated with silver nitrate and mupirocin ointment. A fasting hypoglycemia work-up was completed, with labs drawn during a monitored fast before resuming feeds. She remained stable with blood glucose levels between 55 and 110, and was discharged home with new medications including octreotide and acarbose, instructions for wound care, and follow-up with her endocrinologist.
